reason: The court held the delegated local-authority power remained, but the statement omits the material limits that the construction be within the authority's purview and within the private-interest delegated category.
The court relied on non-party status to refuse restitutio, but the quote is from Perera v Wijewickrama and the statement omits laches, boundary uncertainty, and alternative-remedy qualifications.
The court directly construed Partition Law section 70 and set aside the dismissal because the District Court had not compelled parties or checked whether another defendant would prosecute.
The alternative-remedy point was part of the holding, but the supporting quote is a quotation from Perera v Abeywickrema rather than this court's own statement.
The court directly applied Partition Law section 5 and held that a person who had divested all right, title, and interest before institution was not a necessary party.
The court only found a serious question for interim-injunction purposes and left ownership after striking off to trial, so the extracted statement is too final and underqualified.

The court partly interfered with the partition decrees, but the supplied quote is a held-note from cited precedent and the statement omits the agreed limited exclusion and no-title-rights qualification.
The quote accurately states the case-specific prejudice found, but it is a factual conclusion rather than a reusable ratio or legal rule.
The court accepted that revision and restitutio survived the partition legislation, but the quote is from Somawathie and the statement drops the extraordinary fit-case/miscarriage-of-justice limit.
The passage is a quotation from Iththapana on void proceedings, while this court found summons had been served and dismissed the restitutio application.
The court construed the VAT Act reason-giving requirement, found the assessor's letter gave no reasons, and annulled the assessment.

The discretionary derequisition rule was the holding, but the cited statute ID points to the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance instead of section 10 of the Cooperative Societies special provisions legislation.
The court applied the statutory cancellation procedure, but the supplied quote is from Kalu Banda rather than this court's own supporting reasoning.
The quote is from Podimahatthya and the present court dismissed the writ application after finding the acquisition was lawful and not unreasonable.
The court held that a valid permit-stage nomination by endorsement survived the later grant unless cancelled or revoked and quashed the contrary successor entry.
The court quashed the compensation decision because the respondents failed to give adequate reasons or material support for the valuation.

The court held the original lessee's consent was enough for the lease transfer, but the quote does not support the no-heir-consent part and section 11 of the State Lands Ordinance was not the provision construed for that rule.

The power-of-attorney irregularity holding is real, but the statement omits ratification, lack of prejudice, and later tender of the power, and the cited section should have been Civil Procedure Code section 25(b), not section 17.

The proposition was applied, but the quote is from Virasinghe and the statute ID wrongly points to Prevention of Frauds section 2 rather than the partition-law provisions actually governing necessary parties.
The Supreme Court held that Lot 5 was the only access road to the defendants' Lot 4 and therefore they were entitled to use it on the basis of necessity.
The Supreme Court held that the pleaded delict was setting the law in motion arising from arrest and remand, so section 9 prescribed the action two years after arrest.
The Supreme Court expressly answered that the High Court could not order a retrial without setting aside the District Court judgment.
The court applied the co-owner possession principle, but the supplied quote is from Corea v Appuhami and the extracted statement omits the material ouster exception.
The forfeiture-discretion rule was part of the holding, but the supplied quote only supports discretion and not the stated inquiry into owner knowledge.
The section 533 testamentary-procedure rule was the holding, but the selected quote is too narrow and does not itself support the condition that objections require issues to be framed.
